prompt: According to the course description, which of these is NOT one of the areas this course covers?
explanation: The course description lists the relationship between hardware and software, the organization of the CPU, memory hierarchy, input/output mechanisms, instruction execution, and performance measurement. Databases belong to a different course.

why.a: Wrong, it is covered. The organization of the CPU is named in the course description.
why.b: Wrong, it is covered. Memory hierarchy is named in the course description and gets a whole deck of its own.
why.c: Correct. Database normalisation appears nowhere in the course description; this course is about hardware structure and how programs execute on it.
why.d: Wrong, it is covered. Performance measurement closes the list in the course description.

prompt: The course description says students will learn how computers are designed, how they execute programs, and how architectural choices affect system performance.
explanation: That is the closing sentence of the course description, and it is a good statement of what the whole course is for.

why.true: Correct. All three clauses appear in the course description word for word.
why.false: Wrong. The sentence is in the course description; nothing in it is added or changed.

prompt: Which book heads the recommended textbook list, described as one of the most widely used undergraduate textbooks?

options.text: Structured Computer Organization by Andrew S. Tanenbaum
Computer Organization and Architecture by William Stallings
Computer Organization and Design by Patterson and Hennessy
Essentials of Computer Organization and Architecture by Null and Lobur

explanation: Stallings is number 1 on the list, 11th Edition, Pearson Education, 2019, and it carries the note about being one of the most widely used undergraduate textbooks.

why.a: Wrong. Tanenbaum is number 3 on the list, 6th Edition, 2013.
why.b: Correct. Stallings is number 1, and the widely used note is attached to it.
why.c: Wrong. Patterson and Hennessy is number 2, with ARM and MIPS versions available.
why.d: Wrong. Null and Lobur is number 4 on the list.

prompt: The recommended Stallings text is the {{1}} Edition, published by Pearson Education in {{2}}.
explanation: Stallings, 11th Edition, Pearson Education, 2019. The other years on the list belong to other books: 2013 is Tanenbaum, 2017 and later is Patterson and Hennessy, 2025 is Shiva.

prompt: Match each recommended textbook to its author or authors.

pairs.left: Computer Organization and Design: The Hardware/Software Interface
pairs.right: David A. Patterson and John L. Hennessy

pairs.left: Essentials of Computer Organization and Architecture

explanation: All five recommended texts in one pass. Note how close the titles are to each other: three of the five contain both the words organization and architecture, so the author is the reliable handle.

prompt: Which recommended textbook is available in ARM and MIPS versions?

options.text: Computer Organization and Design: The Hardware/Software Interface

explanation: The Patterson and Hennessy entry is the one whose editions are noted as ARM or MIPS versions, which fits a book that teaches through a concrete instruction set.

why.a: Correct. The list notes 5th and 6th Edition, ARM or MIPS versions available, against Patterson and Hennessy.
why.b: Wrong. Tanenbaum is listed as one edition, the 6th, with no instruction set variants.
why.c: Wrong. Stallings is listed as the 11th Edition only.
why.d: Wrong. Shiva is listed as the 6th Edition, CRC Press, with no instruction set variants.

prompt: The introduction says that increased efficiency, through automation and organization, only scratches the surface of what computing technology has afforded humanity.
explanation: Word for word from the unit introduction. The point is that the effect of computing runs wider than efficiency alone.

why.true: Correct. That is the second sentence of the unit introduction.
why.false: Wrong. The sentence is present and unaltered.

prompt: According to the introduction, what is the position of people who do not use computing technology in their businesses?

options.text: They are legally required to adopt it

explanation: The introduction says the technology has progressed so much that people not utilizing computing technology in their businesses are at a disadvantage.

why.a: Correct. The word the slide uses is disadvantage.
why.b: Wrong. Cost savings are not mentioned anywhere in the introduction.
why.c: Wrong. The slide's whole point is that they are affected, and negatively.
why.d: Wrong. Nothing in the course speaks of a legal requirement.

prompt: Definition 1 in the deck says a computer is a programmable device that does what three things?
explanation: Definition 1: a computer is a programmable device that stores, retrieves, and processes data. Three verbs, in that order.

why.a: Correct. Stores, retrieves, processes, and the word programmable in front of them.
why.b: Wrong. Accept and produce output belong to Definition 3, and display and print appear in neither.
why.c: Wrong. These are file operations, not the deck's wording.
why.d: Wrong. Nothing about encryption or transmission appears in any of the three definitions.

prompt: Definition 1: a computer is a {{1}} device that stores, retrieves, and processes data.

blanks.hint: one word, it is what makes the device general purpose

explanation: Programmable is the load-bearing word in Definition 1. Electronic belongs to Definition 3, sophisticated electronic calculating machine.

prompt: Definition 2 says a computer performs processes, calculations and operations based on instructions provided by what?
explanation: Definition 2 says the instructions are provided by a software or hardware program. Both words matter, because instructions can be wired as well as loaded.

why.a: Correct. Software or hardware program is the deck's phrase.
why.b: Wrong. The operating system is not mentioned in any of the three definitions.
why.c: Wrong. The user is nowhere in Definition 2.
why.d: Wrong. The internally stored list of instructions is Definition 3, not Definition 2.

prompt: Definition 2: a computer is a {{1}} that performs processes, calculations and operations based on instructions provided by a {{2}}.
explanation: Definition 2 in its own words. Programmable device is Definition 1 and calculating machine is Definition 3, so the three definitions are told apart by their opening noun.

prompt: In Definition 3, according to what does the computer process the data it accepts?

options.text: A list of internally stored instructions
The control signals of the peripherals
The order in which the data arrived

explanation: Definition 3: a sophisticated electronic calculating machine that accepts data, processes the data according to a list of internally stored instructions and produces the resulting output information.

why.a: Correct. A list of internally stored instructions is the phrase, and it is the stored program idea in plain words.
why.b: Wrong. That phrasing belongs to Definition 2.
why.c: Wrong. Control signals are an organizational attribute, and they appear later in the deck.
why.d: Wrong. Arrival order is nowhere in the definition.

prompt: Definition 3 calls a computer a sophisticated electronic {{1}} machine that accepts data and produces the resulting output information.

blanks.hint: one word, and it is deliberately old fashioned

explanation: Calculating. Definition 3 is the longest of the three and the only one that names input, processing and output as three separate stages.

prompt: Select the basic components that, according to the deck, all personal computers consist of.
explanation: Five components: CPU, memory, circuit board, storage, and input/output devices. The list is entirely hardware, which is why the operating system is not on it.

why.a: Correct, it is on the list and heads it.
why.b: Correct, memory is second on the list.
why.c: Correct, and it is the one most often forgotten, because it is the board rather than a part mounted on it.
why.d: Correct, storage is listed separately from memory.
why.e: Correct, input/output devices close the list.
why.f: Wrong. The operating system is software; the slide lists the basic hardware components only.

prompt: The deck says all personal computers consist of the same {{1}} basic components.

blanks.hint: count them: CPU, memory, circuit board, storage, input/output

explanation: Five. Losing count usually means folding storage into memory, or dropping the circuit board, which is the easiest one to overlook.

topic: why the personal computer is the example
prompt: Almost every digital device uses the same set of basic components, so examining the personal computer gives insight into the structure of a variety of digital devices.
explanation: This is why the deck teaches from the personal computer: the parts generalise. The same idea returns later, when microcontrollers in washing machines and cars turn out to use Harvard architecture.

why.true: Correct. The slide says almost every digital device uses the same set of components.
why.false: Wrong. The slide makes exactly this claim, and it is the reason the personal computer is used as the worked example.

prompt: According to the deck, what does thinking about computers in terms of their basic components, and the functionality associated with each, reveal?

options.text: The primary functions of the computer in general
The cost of building a computer
The instruction set of the processor
The best operating system for the machine

explanation: The slide's own conclusion: it reveals the primary functions of the computer in general.

why.a: Correct. Primary functions of the computer in general is the slide's phrase.
why.b: Wrong. Cost appears later, as a memory design constraint, not here.
why.c: Wrong. The instruction set is an architectural attribute, taught further down the deck.
why.d: Wrong. Operating systems appear only in the ISA compatibility example.

prompt: Computer systems are designed using which two closely related but distinct concepts?

options.text: Von Neumann design and Harvard design
The instruction set and the microarchitecture

explanation: Architecture and organization. They are the two halves the whole first unit is built on, and the deck is careful to call them closely related but distinct.

why.a: Correct. These are the two concepts the slide names.
why.b: Wrong. Hardware and software is a different division; both concepts here are about the machine.
why.c: Wrong. Von Neumann and Harvard are two system designs, and they sit inside architecture as one component of it.
why.d: Wrong. This is a real distinction but not the one the slide draws; the microarchitecture is not named in this deck.

prompt: Computer architecture and computer organization define how a computer system {{1}} and operates internally.
explanation: Functions and operates internally. The pairing is deliberate: functions points at architecture, operates internally points at organization.

prompt: Computer architecture refers simply to the attributes of a computer that are:

options.text: Visible only to the circuit designer

explanation: Architecture is the attributes visible to a programmer, that is, those with a direct impact on the logical execution of a program. Transparent to the programmer is the opposite phrase, and it defines organization.

why.a: Correct. Visible to a programmer is the definition, and the test of visibility is impact on the logical execution of a program.
why.b: Wrong, and dangerously close. Transparent to the programmer is the phrase used for organizational attributes such as control signals.
why.c: Wrong. Nothing in the definition restricts architecture to the circuit designer.
why.d: Wrong. Benchmarks measure performance, which is an outcome of organization.

prompt: Architectural attributes are those that have a direct impact on the logical execution of a computer program.
explanation: That is the test the deck gives for whether an attribute is architectural. If a program can tell the difference, it is architecture.

why.true: Correct. Direct impact on the logical execution of a computer program is the deck's own test.
why.false: Wrong. This is the definition given, immediately after attributes visible to a programmer.

prompt: In the deck's worked example, deciding whether a multiply instruction is implemented by a special multiply unit or by repeated use of the add unit is:

options.text: Neither, it is a compiler issue

explanation: Whether the machine HAS a multiply instruction is architectural, because a program can see it. HOW that instruction is built is organizational, because the program cannot tell.

why.a: Correct. The implementation choice is invisible to the program, so it is organizational.
why.b: Wrong. The architectural half of this example is whether the computer will have a multiply instruction at all.
why.c: Wrong. The compiler is not part of this example; both halves are machine design decisions.
why.d: Wrong. The example exists precisely to separate the two, so it cannot be both.

prompt: Whether a computer will have a multiply instruction at all is an architectural design issue.
explanation: Yes. The presence of the instruction changes what a programmer can write, so it is architecture. Only its implementation is organization.

why.true: Correct. The deck states it as an architectural design issue in exactly these terms.
why.false: Wrong. You may be thinking of the second half of the example, which is how the instruction is implemented, and that half is organizational.

prompt: Select the aspects of a computer that computer architecture describes, according to the deck.
explanation: Four items: instruction set, data types, addressing modes, register organization. Control signals and memory technology are the deck's own examples of ORGANIZATIONAL attributes, listed a few slides later.

why.a: Correct, and it heads the list.
why.b: Correct, data types is second.
why.c: Correct, addressing modes is third.
why.d: Correct, register organization closes the list of four.
why.e: Wrong. Control signals are named as an organizational attribute, transparent to the programmer.
why.f: Wrong. The memory technology used is also named as an organizational attribute.

prompt: Computer architecture refers to the {{1}} of a computer system.
explanation: Functional design and logical structure. The three wrong choices are all real phrases from the deck, but every one of them defines organization instead.

prompt: Computer architecture answers which question?

options.text: How does the computer do it?
How fast does the computer do it?
How much does the computer cost?

explanation: What does the computer do. That is the single cleanest handle on the whole distinction, and the exam has used it.

why.a: Correct. Architecture answers what, and therefore serves as a blueprint for system design.
why.b: Wrong. How does the computer do it is the question organization answers.
why.c: Wrong. Speed is a result of organization, not the question architecture is said to answer.
why.d: Wrong. Cost is never given as the question either concept answers.

prompt: Because it answers what the computer does, computer architecture serves as a {{1}} for system design.
explanation: Blueprint. It pairs with the building analogy two slides later: architecture is the design, organization is the construction.

prompt: Select the examples of architectural attributes the deck gives.

options.text: The number of bits used to represent various data types
The clock speed of the processor

explanation: Four examples: the instruction set, the number of bits used for data types such as numbers and characters, I/O mechanisms, and techniques for addressing memory.

why.a: Correct, the instruction set is the first example.
why.b: Correct, and the slide spells out the data types as numbers and characters.
why.c: Correct, I/O mechanisms is the third example.
why.d: Correct, techniques for addressing memory closes the list.
why.e: Wrong. Clock speed is never listed as architectural; two machines of the same architecture can differ in clock speed, which is the point of the laptop example later in the deck.

prompt: When the deck lists the number of bits used to represent various data types as an architectural attribute, which examples of data types does it give?
explanation: Numbers and characters, given in brackets on the slide. Both get whole sections of the data representation deck later.

why.a: Correct. The slide's bracket reads numbers, characters.
why.b: Wrong. Pointers are never named as a data type in this deck.
why.c: Wrong. Graphics come much later, in the data representation deck, and are not the example here.
why.d: Wrong. Signed and unsigned are two ways of representing numbers, not the two examples given here.

prompt: The in-class question that follows the architecture slides asks:

options.text: What is the primary focus of computer architecture?
Why were CISC architectures initially popular?
Why do we not use only cache memory?

explanation: The architecture section closes with this in-class question, and the answer slide follows it immediately.

why.a: Correct. This is the in-class question on the architecture side.
why.b: Wrong. That is the in-class question that closes the organization section, four slides later.
why.c: Wrong. That question belongs to the RISC and CISC deck.
why.d: Wrong. That question belongs to the memory hierarchy deck.

prompt: The answer slide says computer architecture focuses on:

options.text: The functional behavior and logical design of the computer system
The physical arrangement and implementation of hardware components
The speed and battery life of the system
The control signals passing between components

explanation: Functional behavior and logical design. Set it beside the organization answer slide, physical arrangement and implementation, and the pair is easy to hold.

why.a: Correct. This is the answer slide word for word.
why.b: Wrong. That is the answer to the other in-class question, the one about organization.
why.c: Wrong. Speed and battery life are what organization determines in the smartphone example.
why.d: Wrong. Control signals are an organizational attribute.

prompt: According to the answer slide, the primary focus of computer architecture is the physical arrangement of hardware components.
explanation: That sentence describes organization. Architecture focuses on the functional behavior and logical design of the system.

why.true: Wrong. Physical arrangement and implementation of hardware components is the answer given for organization, not architecture.
why.false: Correct. Architecture is functional behavior and logical design; the physical arrangement belongs to organization.

prompt: Computer organization refers to the operational units and their interconnections that:

options.text: Serve as a blueprint for system design

explanation: Realize the architectural specifications. The word realize is what makes organization second in order: architecture specifies, organization realizes.

why.a: Correct. Operational units and their interconnections that realize the architectural specifications is the definition.
why.b: Wrong. The instruction set is defined by architecture, not organization.
why.c: Wrong. Visible to a programmer defines architecture; organizational details are transparent to the programmer.
why.d: Wrong. The blueprint is architecture. Organization is the construction.

prompt: Computer organization refers to the operational units and their interconnections that {{1}} the architectural specifications.
explanation: Realize. Architecture defines and describes; organization realizes what has been defined.

prompt: Organizational attributes are described as hardware details that are:
explanation: Transparent to the programmer. In this sense transparent means the programmer sees straight through them and cannot tell they are there, which is the opposite of visible.

why.a: Correct, and the word transparent is worth pausing on: it means unseen, not obvious.
why.b: Wrong. Visible to the programmer is the definition of architectural attributes.
why.c: Wrong. The instruction set is itself an architectural attribute.
why.d: Wrong. Organization exists precisely to realize the architecture, so it is not independent of it.

prompt: Select the examples of organizational attributes the deck gives.

options.text: Interfaces between the computer and peripherals

explanation: Three examples: control signals, interfaces between the computer and peripherals, and the memory technology used.

why.a: Correct, control signals is the first example given.
why.b: Correct, interfaces between the computer and peripherals is the second.
why.c: Correct, the memory technology used is the third.
why.d: Wrong. Addressing modes are listed under architecture, in the group with instruction set, data types and register organization.

prompt: Computer organization refers to the physical implementation of the system. Select what the deck says that includes.
explanation: Four items: hardware components, interconnections, control signals, memory structure. Register organization is on the architecture list, which is the trap here.

why.a: Correct, hardware components heads the list.
why.b: Correct, interconnections is second.
why.c: Correct, control signals appears here as well as in the transparent to the programmer sentence.
why.d: Correct, memory structure closes the list.
why.e: Wrong. Register organization belongs to architecture, alongside instruction set, data types and addressing modes.

prompt: Computer organization refers to the {{1}} of the system, including hardware components, interconnections, control signals and {{2}}.
explanation: Physical implementation, and memory structure. The three wrong choices in the second blank are all on the architecture list, so this blank is really asking you which side each item sits on.

prompt: Computer organization answers which question?

options.text: How does the computer do it?
When does the computer do it?

explanation: How does the computer do it. It ensures the architecture is translated into working hardware.

why.a: Correct. Organization answers how.
why.b: Wrong. What does the computer do is the question architecture answers.
why.c: Wrong. Neither concept is defined by who designed the machine.
why.d: Wrong. Timing is not the question either concept is said to answer.

prompt: Computer organization ensures the architecture is {{1}} into working hardware.
explanation: Translated into working hardware. Organization is the step that turns a specification into a machine.

prompt: In the deck's analogy, computer organization is likened to:

options.text: The actual construction of the building

explanation: Architecture is the building design, organization is the actual construction or implementation of the building.

why.a: Correct. Organization is the construction, the part that makes the design real.
why.b: Wrong. The building design is the analogy for architecture.
why.c: Wrong. Regulations are not part of the analogy.
why.d: Wrong. Cost is not part of the analogy.

prompt: Match each concept to the half of the building analogy it stands for.

pairs.right: The actual construction of the building

explanation: The design against the construction. It is the same shape as the blueprint sentence and the what against how pair, so all three can be learned as one idea.

prompt: The in-class question that closes the organization section asks:

options.text: What is the primary focus of computer architecture?
How does the computer do it?
Which components are visible to the programmer?

explanation: The organization section closes with this question, mirroring the one that closed the architecture section.

why.a: Correct. This is the second of the two in-class questions in this deck.
why.b: Wrong. That is the first in-class question, on the architecture side.
why.c: Wrong. That is the question organization is said to answer, not the in-class question asked about it.
why.d: Wrong. No in-class question in this deck is phrased that way.

prompt: The answer slide says computer organization describes:

options.text: The physical arrangement and implementation of hardware components
The functional behavior and logical design of the computer system
The instruction set and the addressing modes
The attributes visible to a programmer

explanation: Physical arrangement and implementation of hardware components. Its twin, on the architecture side, is functional behavior and logical design.

why.a: Correct. This is the answer slide word for word.
why.b: Wrong. That is the answer given for architecture.
why.c: Wrong. Both of those are architectural attributes.
why.d: Wrong. Visible to a programmer is the definition of architecture.

prompt: Computer organization describes the physical arrangement and implementation of hardware components.
explanation: This is the answer slide to the second in-class question, and it is the shortest usable definition of organization in the whole deck.

why.true: Correct. Physical arrangement and implementation of hardware components is the deck's answer.
why.false: Wrong. This is exactly what the answer slide says.

topic: a system, not a collection of parts
prompt: The deck says a computer system is not just a collection of hardware parts but a carefully designed system governed by computer architecture and computer organization.
explanation: That is the opening sentence of the components section, and it sets up why both concepts have to be studied together.

why.true: Correct. Not just a collection of hardware parts is the deck's own phrasing.
why.false: Wrong. The sentence is present and is the whole point of the slide.

prompt: Understanding the components of architecture and organization is said to be crucial for all of these EXCEPT:
explanation: Three reasons are given: designing efficient hardware systems, writing optimized software, improving system performance. Language choice is not one of them.

why.a: Wrong, it is on the list, and it heads it.
why.b: Wrong, it is on the list, phrased as writing optimized software.
why.c: Wrong, it is on the list and closes it.
why.d: Correct. Choosing a programming language appears nowhere in this deck.

prompt: The components of computer architecture are described as typically visible to programmers and as determining:

options.text: How much power the hardware uses

explanation: They determine how software interacts with hardware, which is the same idea as the ISA being the interface between hardware and software.

why.a: Correct. How software interacts with hardware is the slide's phrase.
why.b: Wrong. Speed is determined by organization, as the laptop example shows.
why.c: Wrong. Power and battery life are organizational outcomes in the smartphone example.
why.d: Wrong. Manufacture is not discussed in this deck.

prompt: Computer architecture defines the logical structure and functional behavior of a computer system.
explanation: The same pair of words as the in-class answer slide, in the reverse order: logical structure and functional behavior.

why.true: Correct. Logical structure and functional behavior is the deck's description of what architecture defines.
why.false: Wrong. This is stated directly, and it matches the earlier answer slide.

prompt: In the smartphone example, match each item to the concept that determines it.
explanation: Architecture defines two things here, organization determines three. Notice that everything a user would notice about the phone falls on the organization side.

prompt: In the smartphone example, battery life is determined by:
explanation: Organization determines speed, battery life and multitasking capability. Architecture defines only the instruction set and the data types.

why.a: Correct. Battery life is one of the three organization determines.
why.b: Wrong. Architecture defines the instruction set and data types in this example, nothing else.
why.c: Wrong. The instruction set is on the architecture side of this very example.
why.d: Wrong. Data types are also on the architecture side.

prompt: Two laptops share the x86 architecture but reach different performance levels. According to the deck, what differs between them?

options.text: Cache size, RAM speed and CPU cores

explanation: Same architecture, different organizations: cache size, RAM speed, CPU cores. The result is different performance levels, with no change to what the machines can be asked to do.

why.a: Correct. These three are the organizational differences the slide names.
why.b: Wrong. Instruction set and addressing modes are architectural, and they are the same on both machines by assumption.
why.c: Wrong. Data types and register set are architectural too, so sharing x86 means sharing them.
why.d: Wrong. Sharing an architecture is precisely what makes the same programs run on both.

prompt: Laptops with the same architecture, for example {{1}}, but different organizations in cache size, RAM speed and CPU cores, end up at different {{2}} levels.
explanation: x86, and performance. The example is the cleanest proof that organization is what you feel and architecture is what you can run.

prompt: The conclusion states that while architecture provides the blueprint and capabilities, organization determines:
explanation: Efficiency and performance. The whole unit reduces to this sentence: capabilities from architecture, efficiency from organization.

why.a: Correct. Organization determines efficiency and performance.
why.b: Wrong. Compatibility follows from sharing an architecture, and it is not the word used here.
why.c: Wrong. Correctness and precision belong to the data representation deck.
why.d: Wrong. Cost is discussed as a memory design constraint, not here.

prompt: Architecture provides the {{1}} and capabilities, while organization determines {{2}} and performance.
explanation: Blueprint and capabilities on one side, efficiency and performance on the other. Blueprint reappears here from the earlier what does the computer do slide.

prompt: Understanding both architecture and organization is said to allow all of these EXCEPT:

options.text: Organizations to build high-performance computing solutions
Users to repair their own hardware

explanation: Three groups are named: engineers, programmers and organizations. Users repairing hardware is not among them.

why.a: Wrong, engineers are named first.
why.b: Wrong, programmers are named second.
why.c: Wrong, organizations building high-performance computing solutions closes the list.
why.d: Correct. This appears nowhere in the conclusion.

prompt: From the revision class, match each description to the concept it defines.

pairs.left: The functional design and logical structure of a computer system
The operational units and their interconnections that realize the architectural specifications
Answers: what does the computer do?
Answers: how does the computer do it?
Hardware details transparent to the programmer, such as control signals

explanation: The revision slide puts both definitions side by side. Every phrase here has appeared in an exam question at some point, so the mapping is worth being fluent in.

prompt: In the revision summary, which of these does computer architecture describe?

options.text: Instruction set, data types, addressing modes, register organization
Control signals, peripheral interfaces, memory technology
Cache size, RAM speed, CPU cores

explanation: The revision slide repeats the four aspects from the introduction deck: instruction set, data types, addressing modes, register organization.

why.a: Correct. These are the four aspects architecture describes.
why.b: Wrong. These are the organizational attributes transparent to the programmer.
why.c: Wrong. These are the organizational differences from the laptop example.
why.d: Wrong. These are what organization determines in the smartphone example.

prompt: From the revision class, select the components of COMPUTER ARCHITECTURE.

options.text: System design, Von Neumann and Harvard

explanation: Six components of architecture. The control unit and the system buses are on the organization list, which has six of its own.

why.a: Correct, the ISA heads the architecture list.
why.b: Correct, data types and representation is second.
why.c: Correct, instruction set and format is third.
why.d: Correct, addressing modes is fourth.
why.f: Correct, system design, meaning Von Neumann and Harvard, closes the architecture list.
why.g: Wrong. The control unit heads the ORGANIZATION list.
why.h: Wrong. System buses and interconnections is fifth on the ORGANIZATION list.

prompt: Match each component to the side it belongs on in the revision class listing.

pairs.left: System design, Von Neumann and Harvard

explanation: Six a side. The reliable test is the one from the definitions: if a program can see it, it is architecture; if it is a physical unit doing the work, it is organization.

prompt: From the revision class, select the components of COMPUTER ORGANIZATION.
explanation: Six components of organization: control unit, ALU unit, memory organization, input/output systems, system buses and interconnections, pipelining and parallelism.

why.a: Correct, the control unit heads the list.
why.b: Correct, the ALU unit is second.
why.c: Correct, memory organization is third.
why.d: Correct, input/output systems is fourth.
why.e: Correct, system buses and interconnections is fifth.
why.f: Correct, pipelining and parallelism closes the list.
why.g: Wrong. Addressing modes is fourth on the ARCHITECTURE list.
